Where it began

Pragyan Ojha was born in Bhubaneswar on 5 September 1986. His cricket started at the age of 10 with a summer camp at the Saheed Sporting Club, and before long he was playing junior tournaments for the club and the city. At 14 he moved to Hyderabad, where his coach T. Vijay Paul helped him make the game his career.

He drew early inspiration from Venkatapathy Raju, a fellow left-arm spinner. Ojha made his first-class debut in 2004/05 and represented India at under-19 level.

The player

He bowled orthodox left-arm spin and loved to give the ball air. A fine 2006–07 Ranji Trophy season, 29 wickets from six games, and strong early years in the Indian Premier League earned him a place in India's one-day side in 2008.

His Test debut came against Sri Lanka in Kanpur in November 2009, in what was India's 100th Test win. In 24 Tests up to 2013 he took 113 wickets at 30.27, with seven five-wicket hauls and a best of 6 for 47. His last Test, against West Indies in 2013, was Sachin Tendulkar's final match. Ojha took 10 for 89 in it and was named man of the match, a fine way to share someone else's big day.

What made him special

Flight was his gift: he was happy to toss the ball up and trust it to do the work. It made him a success in the shorter game too. He took four for 21 on his T20 international debut against Bangladesh, won the Purple Cap as the leading wicket-taker in the third IPL season, and was part of three IPL-winning sides. A late-season stint with Surrey in 2011 brought 24 wickets in four games and helped them to promotion.

Batting was another matter. He made 89 runs in his Test career, which left him in the select club of men with more wickets than runs. To be fair, he was not out in 17 of his 27 innings, so the bowlers rarely got rid of him either.

Away from the middle

He played domestic cricket for Hyderabad for more than a decade, then for Bengal and Bihar, and retired from all cricket in February 2020. He went on to become chief selector for India's senior men's team, a fitting job for a man who spent so long reading batsmen.

And finally

He had the odd honour of becoming Muttiah Muralitharan's 800th and last Test wicket. Murali took more Test wickets than anyone in history. Only one can say he was the very last, and Ojha could fairly point out that it took Murali a whole career to get there.
